name: Cloud & SaaS
description: AWS, Microsoft Entra ID and 365, Google Cloud, Okta, Kubernetes and SaaS integrations.

plays.title: Turn on cloud audit logging everywhere
plays.summary: Most cloud investigations die for lack of logs. Turn them on, centralize them and keep them before you need them.
steps: AWS: create an organization CloudTrail covering all regions, plus S3 and Lambda data events for sensitive resources
Azure: send Entra ID sign-in and audit logs and the Azure Activity log to a Log Analytics workspace or SIEM
Google Cloud: enable Data Access audit logs for sensitive services (only BigQuery has them on by default)
Microsoft 365: confirm Purview audit is on and check which license sets your retention period
Send everything to a log archive account or project that workload admins cannot change

plays.title: Pre-provision responder access to every cloud account
plays.summary: Make sure responders can get read-only and forensic access fast, without asking the team whose account may be compromised.
steps: Create a read-only security audit role in every AWS account, Azure subscription and GCP project
Create a separate forensic role that can snapshot disks and share them to the forensics account
Protect both roles with phishing-resistant MFA and alert on every use
Keep two break-glass accounts outside SSO and the main identity provider, and test them each quarter

plays.title: Build an isolated cloud forensics account
plays.summary: A clean account or project to receive snapshots, run analysis instances and store evidence.
steps: Create a dedicated forensics AWS account, Azure subscription or GCP project with no trust to production
Create encryption keys there and document how to re-encrypt and share snapshots into it
Pre-build an analysis image with forensic tools and no outbound internet
Turn on object lock or immutable storage for the evidence bucket

plays.title: Investigate AWS activity in CloudTrail
plays.summary: Work out what a suspect key, user or role did, where, and when.
steps: Filter CloudTrail by the access key ID, user or role session name across all regions
Look for reconnaissance: GetCallerIdentity, ListBuckets, ListUsers, DescribeInstances
Look for persistence: CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, CreateLoginProfile, AttachUserPolicy, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy
Look for defense evasion: StopLogging, DeleteTrail, PutEventSelectors, DeleteDetector
Check for activity in regions you do not use and for RunInstances of large or GPU instance types
Record source IPs and user agents, then pivot on them across the organization

plays.title: Investigate Entra ID sign-in and audit logs
plays.summary: Find how a Microsoft cloud identity was compromised and what the attacker changed in the tenant.
steps: Review interactive and non-interactive sign-ins for the user: IPs, ASNs, user agents, device IDs, risk detections
Look for token replay: the same session ID used from new IPs or devices
Check audit logs for MFA method changes, device registrations, and new app credentials or role assignments
Check for new or changed Conditional Access policies, federation settings and custom domains
Export the evidence before it ages out (sign-in logs are kept 30 days on P1/P2 licenses, 7 days without them)

plays.title: Search the Microsoft 365 unified audit log
plays.summary: Reconstruct mailbox, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams activity for a compromised user.
steps: Search the unified audit log for the user over the suspected window, and widen it if you find earlier activity
Mail: New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule, UpdateInboxRules, Set-Mailbox (forwarding), Add-MailboxPermission, Send
MailItemsAccessed shows which messages were read; check it is being recorded for the mailbox under your license
Files: FileDownloaded, FileAccessed, FileSyncDownloadedFull and SharingSet/AnonymousLinkCreated on SharePoint and OneDrive
Apps: "Consent to application" and "Add service principal credentials"

plays.title: Investigate Google Cloud audit logs
plays.summary: Trace what a Google Cloud principal did across projects.
steps: Query Admin Activity logs for the principal across the organization
Look for SetIamPolicy calls, service account key creation (CreateServiceAccountKey) and new service accounts
Check for compute instances created in unusual zones and firewall rule changes
Review Data Access logs for storage and BigQuery reads, if they were enabled
Check Security Command Center findings for the same window

plays.title: Investigate the Okta System Log
plays.summary: Find attacker sessions and admin changes in Okta, and everything downstream they reached.
steps: Filter the System Log by user and by suspect IPs, ASNs and user agents
Look for user.session.start from new locations and sessions without the usual device context
Look for factor resets and deactivations (user.mfa.factor.reset_all, user.mfa.factor.deactivate)
Look for admin changes: user.account.privilege.grant, system.api_token.create, policy.lifecycle.update
List the apps the attacker session opened, then investigate each of those apps' own logs

plays.title: Investigate a secret exposed in code
plays.summary: A key, token or password was committed to a repository, pasted somewhere public, or found by secret scanning.
steps: Identify the secret type, what it can reach, and its privilege level
Find the first commit or paste that exposed it and whether the repo or paste was public
Search provider logs for any use of the secret since exposure, especially from IPs outside your ranges
Check for copies in forks, CI logs, build artifacts and container images
Decide whether you are dealing with exposure only or exposure plus use; that decides the scale of response

plays.title: Investigate a compromised SaaS integration
plays.summary: A third-party app connected by OAuth was breached, and its tokens were used against your tenant.
steps: List the integration's OAuth grants, scopes and service accounts in each SaaS platform it connects to
Pull API logs for those tokens. Look for bulk exports, queries for credentials, and access from new IPs
Search data the attacker could read (cases, notes, tickets) for embedded secrets such as API keys and passwords
Check the vendor's advisory for indicators and time windows
Find every other system that trusts the integration's credentials

plays.title: Determine cloud storage data access
plays.summary: Work out exactly which objects were listed, read or copied from cloud storage.
steps: AWS: use CloudTrail S3 data events or S3 server access logs: GetObject, ListObjects, and CopyObject to external buckets
Azure: use Storage diagnostic logs (StorageRead) and check for SAS token use from unknown IPs
Google Cloud: use Data Access logs for storage.objects.get and storage.objects.list
Check bucket policies and ACLs for recent public or cross-account grants
Turn bytes and object counts into a list of affected data for counsel

plays.title: Investigate cryptomining or resource hijacking
plays.summary: A billing spike, quota alert or provider notice suggests someone is running workloads on your bill.
steps: Find new compute: large and GPU instances, container tasks, serverless functions, in every region
Identify the principal that created them and how it got credentials
Check outbound connections from new instances to mining pools
Open a case with the provider early; they may adjust charges for documented abuse
Check quota and spending alerts were in place, and why they did not fire sooner

plays.title: Investigate a Kubernetes workload compromise
plays.summary: Work out how an attacker got into a cluster and what they reached from there.
steps: Pull Kubernetes audit logs. Look for pods/exec, new privileged or hostPath pods, and new ClusterRoleBindings
Check which service account tokens the compromised pod could read, and their RBAC rights
Check whether the pod could reach the cloud metadata service and use the node's cloud identity
Review runtime alerts and container images for unexpected binaries
Capture pod and node state before anything restarts

plays.title: Disable exposed AWS access keys and sessions
plays.summary: Cut off a leaked or misused IAM key, including any temporary credentials already minted with it.
steps: Deactivate the key: aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive (keep it, do not delete yet)
Attach a deny-all policy to the user so session tokens minted with the key stop working too
For roles, use "Revoke active sessions" to deny tokens issued before now
Check for and disable any other keys, users or login profiles the attacker created
Tell application owners first if the key is in production use, and have a replacement ready

plays.title: Quarantine a compromised cloud instance
plays.summary: Isolate a VM without destroying the evidence on it.
steps: Enable termination protection and tag the instance as under investigation
Swap its security groups or NSG for one with no inbound or outbound rules
Snapshot all disks and share the snapshots to the forensics account; capture memory if your tooling allows
Revoke the sessions of the instance role or managed identity; already-issued credentials stay valid until they expire
Deregister it from load balancers and auto scaling so it is not replaced or killed

plays.title: Revoke Entra ID sessions and app credentials
plays.summary: Kick an attacker out of a Microsoft tenant and close the doors they added.
steps: Reset the user's password and revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession)
Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire (60 to 90 minutes by default) unless continuous access evaluation applies; plan for that gap
Remove MFA methods and devices the attacker registered, then require re-registration
Remove credentials (secrets and certificates) added to app registrations and service principals
Revoke admin consent for malicious apps and disable their service principals

plays.title: Lock down exposed cloud storage
plays.summary: Stop ongoing access to buckets, containers or shares that were opened up.
steps: AWS: turn on S3 Block Public Access at account level and remove public or cross-account bucket policies
Azure: disable anonymous blob access and rotate storage account keys to kill SAS tokens signed with them
Google Cloud: remove allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers bindings and enforce public access prevention
Record the policies before you change them, for the timeline

plays.title: Apply organization-level guardrails
plays.summary: Use the cloud's top-level policy to stop an attacker even if they hold admin rights in an account.
steps: AWS: apply a service control policy to deny unused regions and IAM changes except from the break-glass role
Azure: use management group policy and deny assignments to block risky resource types and regions
Google Cloud: use organization policies to restrict service account key creation and resource locations
Test the guardrails on a non-production account first if time allows

plays.title: Revoke compromised SaaS integration tokens
plays.summary: Cut the connection between a breached third-party app and your SaaS tenants.
steps: Revoke the integration's OAuth tokens and disable its connected app in each platform
Rotate any API keys or service account passwords stored in or for the integration
Rotate secrets the attacker may have read from SaaS data, such as keys pasted into tickets
Tell the business owner which workflows will break until the vendor gives the all-clear

plays.title: Isolate a compromised Kubernetes workload
plays.summary: Stop a compromised pod spreading without losing the evidence on it.
steps: Apply a deny-all NetworkPolicy to the pod's labels; keep the pod running
Cordon the node so nothing new is scheduled there
Remove the pod's service account RBAC bindings and rotate any secrets it mounted
Block the pod and node from the cloud metadata endpoint if it was not already blocked

plays.title: Remove attacker persistence in cloud IAM
plays.summary: Cloud attackers persist through identities, not files. Find and remove every foothold.
steps: AWS: review new users, keys, roles with external trust, Lambda functions, EventBridge rules and identity providers
Entra ID: review new app credentials, federated domains, service principals with high privileges and guest users
Google Cloud: review service account keys, IAM bindings on folders and the organization, and workload identity pools
Compare against IaC or a known-good snapshot of IAM, not just your memory of it

plays.title: Rotate secrets the attacker could read
plays.summary: Assume every secret reachable by the compromised identity is now known to the attacker.
steps: List secrets in Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Key Vault and Secret Manager the identity could read
Check the access logs to see which ones were actually read
Rotate the read secrets first, then the rest, in order of business impact
Update dependent applications and confirm they still work

plays.title: Redeploy cloud workloads from known-good code
plays.summary: Replace compromised instances, containers and functions instead of cleaning them.
steps: Rebuild from infrastructure-as-code and images built before the compromise
Verify image digests and pipeline integrity before redeploying
Use fresh credentials and keys for the new deployment
Keep the old resources quarantined until the investigation closes

plays.title: Restore cloud data from versions and backups
plays.summary: Bring back deleted or encrypted cloud data from protected copies.
steps: Restore from S3 versioning or Object Lock, Azure soft delete, or GCS object versioning
For databases, restore to a point in time before the attacker's first action
Restore into a new resource, validate it, then switch traffic
Confirm the backups were not reachable by the compromised identity before trusting them

plays.title: Validate cloud posture before closing
plays.summary: Confirm the environment is back to a secure baseline across every account.
steps: Run a posture scan (Security Hub, Defender for Cloud, Security Command Center, or Prowler)
Confirm logging, GuardDuty or Defender plans, and alerting are back on everywhere
Re-check public exposure of storage, snapshots and AMIs
Review spending for a week to catch leftover attacker resources

plays.title: Turn the cloud attack path into guardrails
plays.summary: Make the same path impossible, not just detectable.
steps: Map each attacker step to the control that would have stopped it
Prefer preventive org-level policies over per-account fixes
Add detections for the API calls you saw, tested against replayed logs
Remove long-lived keys where workload identity or federation can replace them

templates.description: An IAM access key was leaked or GuardDuty flagged its use from outside your environment.
nodes: Exposure only: still rotate the key, scrub the secret from history, and record why no further action was needed.
